title: Of coaches
paragraphs: It is easy enough to see that the great authors, when they write of causes, do not stick to the ones they actually think are true — they reach for any that strike them as elegant or inventive. They speak truthfully and usefully so long as they speak ingeniously. We cannot make ourselves certain of the supreme cause, so we crowd a great many together, on the chance that the right one may be in the heap somewhere:
"Namque unam dicere causam Non satis est, verum plures, unde una tamen sit."
[Lucretius, vi. 704. — The sense is given in the preceding passage.]

Do you ask me where the custom of blessing those who sneeze comes from? We break wind three different ways. The one that escapes from below is too foul; the one that comes out of the mouth carries a hint of gluttony; the third is sneezing, and because it issues from the head and is no offence to anyone, we give it a polite welcome. Don't laugh at the distinction — they say it is Aristotle's.

I think I have seen in Plutarch (who of all the authors I know has best mixed art with nature and judgment with learning) that he gives as the reason for the heaving of the stomach in people at sea that it is caused by fear, having first worked out some chain of reasoning by which he proves fear can have such an effect. I, who am very prone to seasickness, know perfectly well this cause does not apply to me — and I know it not by argument but by necessary experience. Without even bringing in what I have been told, that the same thing often happens to animals, especially pigs, who have no notion of danger; or what an acquaintance of mine told me about himself, that though he was very subject to it, the urge to vomit left him three or four times when he was badly frightened in a violent storm, just as it did that ancient writer:
"Pejus vexabar, quam ut periculum mihi succurreret;"
["I was too ill to think of danger." (Or in reverse:) "I was too frightened to be ill." — Seneca, Ep., 53. 2]

I was never afraid on the water — nor, for that matter, in any other peril (and I have seen enough that would have qualified, if death is one of them) — so afraid as to be stunned out of my judgment. Fear sometimes springs as much from lack of judgment as from lack of courage. All the dangers I have stood in I have looked at without flinching, with open, sound, full sight; and in truth, a man needs courage to be afraid. It served me better, once, than any other help, in arranging and managing my retreat, so that it was, if not without fear, at least without panic and stupor; agitated, yes, but not bewildered or paralysed. Great souls go much further than this and offer us flights that are not only steady and temperate but actually noble. Let me recount what Alcibiades reports of Socrates, his comrade in arms: "I came across him," he says, "after the rout of our army, him and Lachez, last among those who fled, and I took a long look at him at my leisure and in safety, since I was mounted on a good horse and he was on foot, just as he had fought. The first thing I noticed was how much more judgment and resolve he showed than Lachez, and then the courage of his march, nothing different from his ordinary gait; his eye firm and steady, taking in and judging what was happening around him, glancing now at this man, now at that, friend and enemy, in such a way as to encourage the one and signal to the other that he meant to sell his life dear to anyone who came to take it from him — and so they got away, for people are not eager to attack such men, and prefer to chase those they see are frightened." That is the testimony of this great captain, and it teaches us, what we see every day, that nothing throws us into danger so surely as the headlong eagerness to escape it:
"Quo timoris minus est, eo minus ferme periculi est."
["When there is least fear, there is usually least danger." — Livy, xxii. 5.]

Our people are wrong when they say of a man that he is afraid of death just because he thinks about it and sees it coming. Foresight is just as appropriate in things that touch us, whether good or bad. To weigh and judge a danger is, in some sense, the opposite of being stunned by it. As for myself, I do not feel strong enough to bear up under the force and rush of this passion of fear, or any other intense passion: if I were once conquered and laid out by it, I should never get up sound again. Whoever once made my soul lose its footing would never set her upright again — she tastes and probes herself too deeply, too close to the quick, and so she would never let the wound she had received heal and scar over. It has been my good fortune that no illness has yet thrown her off balance: at every attack made on me I keep up my full opposition and defence, which means the first blow that managed to rout me would prevent me ever rallying. I have no second move to play; whichever side the flood breaks my banks, I lie open and am drowned beyond saving. Epicurus says a wise man can never turn into a fool. I hold the reverse: that whoever has once been a thoroughgoing fool will never afterwards be very wise. God gives me cold weather according to my cloak, and passions in proportion to the means I have to resist them: nature, having left me exposed on one side, has covered me on the other; having stripped me of strength, she has armed me with insensibility and a steady — call it dull, if you like — apprehension.

I cannot now stand for long (and when I was young could stand still less) either coach, litter, or boat. I hate every kind of transport except on horseback, both in town and country. But I can bear a litter worse than a coach; and, by the same logic, a rough rocking on the water, where it provokes fear, better than the motion of a calm. The little jerks of oars stealing the boat from under us — I cannot say how, but I find both my head and my stomach upset by them. Nor can I bear to sit on a wobbly chair. When the sail or the current carries us evenly, or we are being towed, the even motion does not bother me at all. It is interrupted motion that upsets me, and most of all when it is slowest; I cannot put it any better than that. The physicians have told me to squeeze and tighten myself round the lower belly with a napkin to remedy this trouble; but I haven't tried it, being used to wrestling with my own defects and overcoming them myself.

If my memory were better, I would not think it time wasted to set down here the endless variety that history offers us of the use of chariots in war — varying with the nations and the age, in my view of great usefulness and effect, so that it is a wonder we have lost all knowledge of them. I will say only this, that very recently, in our fathers' time, the Hungarians made excellent use of them against the Turks: in each one a shield-bearer and a musketeer, and a number of harquebuses stacked ready and loaded, and the whole covered with a pavise like a galliot. They formed the front of their line with three thousand such coaches, and after the cannon had fired they made them all pour their shot into the enemy, who had to swallow that volley before getting to the rest, which was no small advantage; that done, these chariots charged into the enemy squadrons to break them and open a way for the rest. Beyond that, there is the use that might be made of them to flank the soldiers in dangerous country when marching, or to cover a position and fortify it in a hurry. In my own time a gentleman on one of our frontiers, too unwieldy of body to find any horse able to carry his weight, was in a quarrel and rode through the country in a chariot of this kind, and found it very convenient. But let us leave these war chariots.

As if their softness had not been clear enough from better evidence, the last kings of our first race used to travel in a chariot drawn by four oxen. Mark Antony was the first man in Rome to have himself drawn in a coach by lions, with a singing girl beside him.
[Cytheris, the Roman courtesan. — Plutarch's Life of Antony, c. 3. This was the same woman who is introduced by Gallus under the name of Lycoris. Gallus must have known her personally.]

Heliogabalus did the same later on, calling himself Cybele, the mother of the gods, and was also drawn by tigers, taking on the role of the god Bacchus; he sometimes harnessed two stags to his coach, another time four dogs, and another four naked girls, having himself drawn by them in procession, stark naked too. The Emperor Firmus had his chariot drawn by ostriches of a prodigious size, so that it seemed to fly rather than roll.

The strangeness of these inventions puts another thought in my head: that it is a kind of weakness in monarchs, and evidence that they don't sufficiently understand what they are, when they go in for being honoured and looking great through extravagant expense. It might be forgivable in a foreign country, but among their own subjects, where they hold sovereign power and can do whatever they like, it takes away from their dignity at the very pinnacle of honour they can reach: just as, it seems to me, it is unnecessary for a private gentleman to dress lavishly at home — his house, his servants, his kitchen answer for him well enough. The advice Isocrates gives his king seems to me grounded in reason: that he should be splendid in plate and furniture, because it is an expense of long duration that passes on to his successors, and that he should avoid all kinds of grandeur that will soon be forgotten. I loved to dress finely when I was a younger brother, for want of any other ornament, and it suited me well; there are some on whom rich clothes practically weep. We have strange stories of the personal frugality of our kings — kings who were great in reputation, courage, and fortune. Demosthenes was passionately against the law of his city that set aside public money for the splendour of their public games and festivals: he wanted their greatness to be displayed in numbers of well-equipped ships and well-provisioned armies; and there is good reason to condemn Theophrastus, who in his Book on Riches takes the contrary view, holding that sort of expense to be the true fruit of abundance. These are pleasures, says Aristotle, that please only the lower sort of people and vanish from memory as soon as the crowd has had its fill, and no serious or judicious man can have any respect for them. This money would, in my opinion, be much more royally — and also more usefully, justly, and lastingly — spent on ports, harbours, walls, and fortifications, on grand buildings, churches, hospitals, colleges, and on the improvement of streets and highways — and Pope Gregory XIII will leave a fine memory to future ages for just this; and our Queen Catherine would have left to posterity proof of her natural generosity and munificence, had her means matched her inclinations. Fortune has done me a great injury by interrupting the noble work on the Pont-Neuf of our great city, and depriving me of the hope of seeing it finished before I die.

On top of that, it seems to the subjects, who are spectators of these triumphs, that their own riches are being spread out before them, and that they are being entertained at their own cost. For people are inclined to assume of kings, as we do of our servants, that they must see to it that all things needful are provided in abundance, but not touch them themselves. So the Emperor Galba, pleased with a musician who played to him at supper, called for his money-box and gave him a handful of crowns out of it, with these words: "This is not the public's money, but my own." Yet it usually turns out that the people have the right of it, and that their princes feed their eyes with what they need to fill their bellies.

Liberality is not even at its true splendour in a sovereign hand: private men have the most genuine claim to it. For, strictly speaking, a king has nothing properly his own; he owes himself to others. Authority is given not for the benefit of the magistrate but of the people; a superior is never made so for his own gain, but for the gain of his inferiors — a physician for the sake of the sick man, not for his own. Every magistracy, like every art, has its end outside itself. Therefore the tutors of young princes who make a point of impressing on them this virtue of liberality, and preach to them to refuse nothing and to consider nothing better spent than what they give away (a doctrine I have seen highly credited in my time), either care more for their own profit than for their master's, or have a poor sense of who they are talking to. It is too easy a thing to drum liberality into someone who has as much as he wants to practise it with at others' expense; and since the value of the gift is set not by its own measure but by the measure of the giver's means, in such mighty hands it comes to nothing — they find themselves wasteful before they can be called liberal. And it is not much of a recommendation, compared with the other royal virtues; it is the only one, as the tyrant Dionysius said, that goes well even with tyranny itself. I would rather teach the prince this line from the ancient farm-worker:
["That whoever wants a good harvest must sow with his hand, not pour out of the sack." — Plutarch, Apothegms, Whether the Ancients were more excellent in Arms than in Learning.]

he must scatter it about, not heap it all in one place. And since he has to give, or rather to pay and to repay so many people in proportion to their deserts, he should be a loyal and discriminating distributor. If a prince's liberality is without measure or discretion, I would rather he were stingy.

Royal virtue seems to consist mostly in justice; and of all the parts of justice, the one that most marks out a king is the liberality that accompanies it, for this is what kings have especially reserved to be done by themselves, whereas all the other forms of justice they leave to be administered by others. An immoderate generosity is a very weak way of acquiring goodwill — it puts off more people than it attracts:
"Quo in plures usus sis, minus in multos uti possis... Quid autem est stultius, quam, quod libenter facias, curare ut id diutius facere non possis;"

["The more people you use it on, the fewer will be left to use it on. And what greater folly can there be than to arrange things so that what you would willingly do, you cannot keep on doing." — Cicero, De Offic., ii. 15.]

And if it is handed out without due respect for merit, it embarrasses the man who receives it, and is received ungraciously. Tyrants have been sacrificed to the people's hatred at the hands of the very men they had wrongfully advanced: the kind of men — buffoons, pimps, fiddlers, and other riff-raff — who, thinking to secure their possession of benefits they did not deserve, take care to display hatred and contempt for the man they hold them from, joining in the common verdict against him.

The subjects of a prince extravagant in giving become extravagant in asking, and set their demands not by reason but by precedent. We have, in all seriousness, very often reason to blush at our own shamelessness: we are overpaid, by any just measure, when the reward matches our service. Don't we already owe our princes something by natural obligation? If he covers our costs, he does too much; it is enough that he contribute to them. The surplus is called a benefit, and a benefit cannot be demanded — for the very word Liberality has Liberty in it.

In our way of doing things, it is never finished; we never count what we have already received; we are only ever looking ahead to the next generosity. So the more a prince empties himself out in giving, the poorer he grows in friends. How could he ever satisfy immoderate desires, which grow with every fulfilment? Someone whose mind is on what he can take never thinks about what he has already taken; covetousness has nothing more properly its own than ingratitude.

The example of Cyrus will not be out of place here, to give the kings of our day a yardstick by which to judge whether their gifts are well or badly bestowed, and to see how much better that emperor handed them out than they do — they who are reduced to borrowing from unknown subjects, and from those they have wronged rather than those on whom they have lavished their benefits, receiving help in which there is nothing free but the name. Croesus reproached Cyrus for his generosity, and worked out how much his treasury would have come to had he been a little tighter-fisted. Cyrus wanted to justify his liberality, and so sent letters out to all the great men of his realm whom he had particularly helped, asking each of them to send him as much money as he could for an urgent need, and to send him the precise amount each could advance. When all these answers came back, every one of his friends — not thinking it enough merely to offer back as much as he had received from his bounty, and adding to it a great deal of his own — it turned out the sum came to a great deal more than Croesus had reckoned. Whereupon Cyrus said: "I am no less in love with riches than other princes, but I am a better steward of them. You see for what a small outlay I have acquired the priceless treasure of so many friends, and how much more faithfully they hold it for me than mercenary men without bond or affection. My money is better stored than in chests — chests that bring with them the hatred, envy, and contempt of other princes."

The emperors excused the extravagance of their games and public spectacles by the fact that their authority depended, in some way (at least in appearance), on the will of the people of Rome, who from time immemorial had been used to being entertained and flattered with such shows and excesses. But it was private citizens who had built up this custom, in order to indulge their fellow citizens and companions, chiefly out of their own pockets, with such lavishness and magnificence — it had quite another flavour when the masters came to imitate it:
"Pecuniarum translatio a justis dominis ad alienos non debet liberalis videri."
["The transferring of money from its rightful owners to outsiders ought not to be called liberality." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 14.]

Philip, seeing that his son was trying to win the affection of the Macedonians by gifts, scolded him in a letter to this effect: "What? Do you want your subjects to look on you as their cashier, not as their king? Are you going to woo them to win their love? Do it, then, by the gifts of your virtue, and not by those of your purse." And yet it was certainly a fine sight to bring in and plant within the amphitheatre a great number of vast trees, with all their branches in full leaf, representing a great shady forest laid out in excellent order; and on the first day, to release into it a thousand ostriches, a thousand stags, a thousand boars, and a thousand fallow-deer, to be killed and disposed of by the people; on the next day, to have a hundred great lions, a hundred leopards, and three hundred bears killed in his presence; and for the third day, to make three hundred pairs of gladiators fight it out to the death, as the Emperor Probus did. It was also very fine to see those vast amphitheatres faced on the outside with marble, intricately worked with figures and statues, and inside glittering with rare ornamentation:
"Baltheus en! gemmis, en illita porticus auro:"
["A belt glittering with jewels, and a portico overlaid with gold." — Calpurnius, Eclog., vii. 47. A baltheus was a shoulder-belt or baldric.]
all the sides of this vast space filled and ringed, from bottom to top, with sixty or eighty rows of seats, also of marble, and covered with cushions:
"Exeat, inquit, Si pudor est, et de pulvino surgat equestri, Cujus res legi non sufficit;"

["Let him go out, he said, if he has any shame, and rise from the equestrian cushion, the man whose estate does not meet the law." — Juvenal, iii. 153. The Equites were required to possess a fortune of 400 sestertia, and they sat on the first fourteen rows behind the orchestra.]

where a hundred thousand men might sit at their ease; and the area below, where the games were played, made to open up first and crack into chasms, representing caves that disgorged the beasts intended for the show; and then, secondly, flooded by a deep sea full of sea-monsters and laden with warships, to stage a naval battle; and, thirdly, made dry and level again for the gladiators' combat; and, for the fourth scene, strewn with vermilion and storax in place of sand, to set out a solemn feast for that whole vast multitude — the last act of one single day:

"Quoties nos descendentis arenae Vidimus in partes, ruptaque voragine terrae Emersisse feras, et eisdem saepe latebris Aurea cum croceo creverunt arbuta libro!.... Nec solum nobis silvestria cernere monstra Contigit; aequoreos ego cum certantibus ursis Spectavi vitulos, et equorum nomine dignum, Sen deforme pecus, quod in illo nascitur amni...."

["How often have we seen the floor of the theatre sink and split apart, and from a chasm in the earth wild beasts emerge, and then in a moment a grove of gilded trees spring up, putting forth blossoms of enamelled flowers. Nor was it only forest marvels we saw: I watched sea-calves fight with bears, and a deformed sort of cattle that one might call sea-horses." — Calpurnius, Eclog., vii. 64.]

Sometimes they made a high mountain rise up, covered with fruit-trees and other leafy trees, sending down little streams of water from the top as if from a fountain's mouth; at other times a great ship was seen rolling in which opened and split apart of itself, and after disgorging from the hold four or five hundred beasts for the fight, closed up again and disappeared without help. At other times, from the floor of this place, they made jets of perfumed water shoot upwards, so high as to sprinkle the whole vast crowd. To shield themselves from the weather, they had this huge space sometimes covered over with purple needlework curtains, and at other times with silk of one colour or another, which they drew off and on at will:
"Quamvis non modico caleant spectacula sole, Vela reducuntur, cum venit Hermogenes."
The netting that was set in front of the people to protect them from the loosed beasts was also woven of gold:
"Auro quoque torts refulgent Retia."
["The woven nets shine with gold." — Calpurnius, ubi supra.]

If there is anything to be said in defence of excesses like these, it is where the novelty and invention strike us more than the cost; even in these vanities we can see how fertile those ages were in another kind of wit than ours. With this sort of fertility it is as with every other product of nature: not that she there spent her utmost force; we don't really go anywhere — we run back and forth, whirl this way and that, turn back the way we came. I am afraid our knowledge is weak in every direction: we see neither far forward nor far back; our understanding takes in little, and lives only a little while; it is short both in extent of time and in extent of matter:
"Vixere fortes ante Agamemnona Mufti, sed omnes illacrymabiles Urgentur, ignotique longs Nocte."
["Many brave men lived before Agamemnon, but all are pressed by the long night, unmourned and unknown." — Horace, Od., iv. 9, 25.]
"Et supra bellum Thebanum et funera Trojae Non alias alii quoque res cecinere poetae?"

["Why, before the Theban war and the destruction of Troy, did no other poets sing of other events?" — Lucretius, v. 327. Montaigne here amuses himself by giving Lucretius' words a sense directly opposite to what they bear in the poem. Lucretius poses the question: why, if the earth had existed from all eternity, were there no poets before the Theban war to sing of men's exploits? — Coste.]

And the account by Solon of what he learned from the Egyptian priests, about the long life of their state and their way of learning and preserving foreign histories, is not, it seems to me, a piece of evidence to be brushed aside on this point:

"Si interminatam in omnes partes magnitudinem regionum videremus et temporum, in quam se injiciens animus et intendens, ita late longeque peregrinatur, ut nullam oram ultimi videat, in qua possit insistere: in haec immensitate . . . infinita vis innumerabilium appareret fomorum."

["If we could see on all sides the unlimited magnitude of regions and of times — into which the mind, pressing in and stretching out, wanders so wide and far that it sees no edge of the limit at which it could come to rest — in that immensity we should perceive an infinite force of innumerable forms." Here too Montaigne gives the words a sense quite different from what they bear in the original; but the application he makes of them is so apt that one would say they had been put together expressly to express his thought. "Et temporum" is an addition by Montaigne. — Coste.]

Even if everything that reached us by report of our knowledge of past ages were true, and were known to some one person, it would still be less than nothing in comparison with what is unknown. And of this same picture of the world, which is slipping past us while we live in it, how feeble and limited is the knowledge of even the most curious — not just of particular events, which fortune often makes exemplary and consequential, but of the state of great governments and nations: a hundred times more escapes us than ever comes to our knowledge. We make a great fuss about the invention of artillery and printing, when other men at the other end of the world, in China, had them a thousand years ago. If we could see as much of the world as we cannot see, we should perceive, we may reasonably believe, a perpetual repetition and variation of forms. Nothing is unique or rare in respect of nature, only in respect of our knowledge, which is a poor foundation on which to base our rules and which presents to us a very false image of things. As today we vainly conclude that the world is in decline and old age from the arguments we draw from our own weakness and decay:
"Jamque adeo est affecta aetas effoet aque tellus;"
["Our age is feeble, and the earth less fertile." — Lucretius, ii. 1151.]
so he vainly concluded as to its birth and youth, from the vigour he observed in the minds of his own time, which were full of novelties and new inventions:
"Verum, ut opinor, habet novitatem summa, recensque Natura est mundi, neque pridem exordia coepit Quare etiam quaedam nunc artes expoliuntur, Nunc etiam augescunt; nunc addita navigiis sunt Multa."

["But in my opinion the whole world is of recent origin, and did not begin in remote times; which is why some arts are still being refined, and some are only just on the rise; and at present many additions are being made to shipping." — Lucretius, v. 331.]

Our world has lately discovered another (and who can assure us it is the last of its siblings, since the daemons, the sibyls, and we ourselves have been ignorant of this one until now?), as large, well-peopled, and fruitful as the one we live on, and yet so raw and young that we are still teaching it its ABC: it is barely fifty years since it knew neither letters, weights, measures, clothes, grain, nor vines; it was still naked in the mother's lap, and lived on what she gave it. If we are right to draw conclusions about our own end, and this poet right about the youthfulness of his own age, that other world will only just be entering into the light when ours makes its exit. The universe will fall into paralysis: one limb will be useless, the other in its vigour. I am very much afraid that we have hugely accelerated its decline and ruin by our contagion, and that we have sold it our opinions and our arts at a very high price. It was an infant world — and yet we did not whip and subject it to our discipline by virtue of our natural worth and strength; nor did we win it over by our justice and goodness, nor master it by our magnanimity. Most of their answers, and of the negotiations we had with them, show that they were in no way behind us in sharpness or clarity of natural understanding. The astonishing magnificence of the cities of Cusco and Mexico, and among many other things the garden of the king, where all the trees, fruits, and plants were perfectly modelled in gold, in the order and stature they would have in a real garden — and in his cabinet were all the animals bred on his territory and in its seas; and the beauty of their craft work in jewels, feathers, cotton, and painting — all give ample proof that in industry they were no less our equals. But as to devotion, observance of laws, goodness, generosity, loyalty, and plain dealing, it served us well that we had less of these than they; for it is by this very advantage of theirs over us that they have lost themselves, sold themselves, betrayed themselves.

As for boldness and courage, steadiness, constancy in the face of pain, hunger, and death, I would not be afraid to set the examples I find among them against the most famous examples of ancient times we find in our own records on this side of the world. As for those who subdued them, take away the tricks and artifices they used to dupe them, and the just astonishment those nations felt at the sudden, unexpected arrival of bearded men, different in language, religion, shape, and face, from a part of the world so remote they had never heard there was any inhabited land there, mounted on great unknown monsters — they who had not only never seen a horse, but had never seen any other beast trained to carry a man or any other load; sheathed in a hard, shining skin, with a cutting and glittering weapon in his hand, against people who, in wonder at the brightness of a mirror or a knife, would exchange great treasures of gold and pearl, and who had neither the knowledge nor the materials with which, given time, they could have penetrated our steel; add to this the lightning and thunder of our cannon and harquebuses, enough to frighten Caesar himself had he been surprised by them with so little experience, set against people naked, except where they used a little quilted cotton, with no other arms at most than bows, stones, sticks, and wooden shields; people taken by surprise under colour of friendship and good faith, by their curiosity to see strange and unknown things — take away, I say, this disparity from the conquerors, and you take away the whole occasion of so many victories. When I look at that unconquerable ardour with which so many thousands of men, women, and children threw themselves over and over again into certain death for the defence of their gods and their freedoms; that noble stubbornness in enduring every extremity and hardship, and death itself, rather than submit to the rule of those by whom they had been so shamefully abused; some of them choosing, when prisoner, to starve themselves to death rather than take food from the hands of enemies who had triumphed so basely — I see that whoever had attacked them on equal terms of arms, experience, and numbers would have had a hard, and possibly a harder, fight on his hands than in any war we have ever known.

Why did such a noble conquest not fall to Alexander, or to the ancient Greeks and Romans? Why did so great a revolution and upheaval of so many empires and peoples not fall into hands that would gently have levelled and smoothed out what was rough and savage among them, and would have cherished and propagated the good seeds nature had already planted there — mixing not only with the cultivation of the soil and the adornment of cities the arts of this part of the world, in what was necessary, but also the Greek and Roman virtues with those native to the country? What a reparation it would have been to them, what a general good to the whole world, if our first examples and behaviour over there had drawn those people into admiration and imitation of virtue, and had brought into being a brotherhood and mutual understanding between them and us? How easy it would have been to take advantage of souls so innocent, and so eager to learn, having for the most part such naturally good inclinations to start with? Whereas, on the contrary, we took advantage of their ignorance and inexperience with all the more ease to bend them towards treachery, luxury, greed, and every kind of inhumanity and cruelty, by the pattern and example of our own manners. Who has ever set so high a price on his merchandise? So many cities razed to the ground, so many nations exterminated, so many millions of people put to the sword, and the richest and most beautiful part of the world turned upside down, for the sake of trading in pearl and pepper. Mechanical victories! Never did ambition, never did public quarrels, drive men against one another into such miserable hostilities, into such miserable calamities.

Some Spaniards, sailing along the coast in search of their mines, landed in a fertile, pleasant, well-populated country, and there gave the inhabitants their usual speech: "that they were peaceable men, come from a very remote country, sent on behalf of the King of Castile, the greatest prince in the inhabited world, to whom the Pope, God's deputy on earth, had given the sovereignty of the whole of the Indies; that if they would become his tributaries, they would be very gently and courteously treated" — at the same time asking them for provisions for their sustenance, and for gold to make some supposed medicine, and also setting before them the belief in one God only and the truth of our religion, which they advised them to embrace, with a few threats thrown in. To which they got this answer: "As for being peaceable, they did not look it, if that was what they were. As for their king, since he had to go begging, he must be needy and poor; and whoever had made him this gift must be a man who loved trouble, to give to one man what was not his, and so to start a dispute against its long-standing owners. As for provisions, they would supply them. Of gold they had little, since they thought very little of it as having no use in the conduct of life — their only concern was to get through it happily and pleasantly; but what they could find, except what was used in the service of their gods, the Spaniards were welcome to take. As for one God only, they liked the idea well enough; but they had no wish to change their religion, since they had lived in it so long and so happily, and they were not in the habit of taking advice from anyone but their friends, and those they knew. As for their threats, it showed lack of judgment to threaten people whose nature and power were unknown to them. They had better get away from their coast in a hurry, for they were not used to taking the civilities and professions of armed strangers in good part; otherwise they would treat them as they had treated those others" — showing them the heads of several executed men round the walls of their city. A fine example of the babble of these children! But the upshot was that the Spaniards did not, in this or in several other places where they did not find the merchandise they were after, make any stay or attempt, however many other advantages were to be had there. See my essay on the CANNIBALS.

Of the two most powerful monarchs of that world — and perhaps of this — kings over so many kings, the last they overthrew, the king of Peru, having been taken in battle, was held to so excessive a ransom as goes beyond belief; and having faithfully paid it, and having shown by his conversation clear signs of a frank, generous, steady spirit and a clear, settled understanding, the conquerors had a mind, after extracting one million three hundred and twenty-five thousand five hundred pounds' weight of gold, along with silver and other things that came to no less (so that their horses were shod with solid gold), to see, at the price of whatever disloyalty and injustice it might cost, what the rest of this king's treasure might be, and to get hold of that too. To this end a false accusation was brought against him, and false witnesses produced to prove that he was trying to stir up a rising in his provinces to recover his own liberty; whereupon, by the virtuous sentence of the very men who by this treachery had plotted his ruin, he was condemned to be publicly hanged and strangled — having first been made to buy himself off the torment of being burned alive by accepting the baptism they gave him just before execution: a horrid and unheard-of barbarity, which he nevertheless underwent without faltering in word or look, with a truly grave and royal bearing. Afterwards, to calm and pacify the people, dismayed and stunned by so strange a thing, they pretended great sorrow at his death, and arranged a most lavish funeral.

The other king, of Mexico, having defended his besieged city for a long time, and having in this siege shown the utmost that endurance and perseverance can do, if ever prince and people did, then having had the misfortune of being delivered alive into his enemies' hands on terms of being treated as a king, did nothing in his captivity unworthy of that title. His enemies, after their victory, not finding as much gold as they had expected, when they had searched and ransacked with their utmost diligence, set about extracting disclosures by the cruellest tortures they could invent on the prisoners they had taken: but having got nothing by these — their courage being greater than their tortures — they at last arrived at such a pitch of fury that, against their pledge and the law of nations, they put the king himself, and one of the chief nobles of his court, to the rack, in the sight of each other. This lord, finding himself overcome by the pain, surrounded by burning coals, pitifully turned his dying eyes towards his master, as if to ask his pardon for being unable to bear any more; whereupon the king, fixing him with a fierce, severe look, as if reproaching his cowardice and pusillanimity, said to him in a harsh, steady voice only this: "And what do you think I am suffering? Am I in a bath? Am I better off than you?" Whereupon the other immediately gave up under the torment and died on the spot. The king, half roasted, was carried away — not so much out of pity (for what compassion ever touched souls so barbarous that, on the doubtful tip about some vessel of gold to be plundered, they had not a man but a king, so great in fortune and worth, broiled before their eyes?) but because his constancy made their cruelty more shameful still. They afterwards hanged him for having nobly tried to free himself by arms from so long a captivity and subjection, and he died with a courage worthy of so great a prince.

Another time, they burned in the same fire four hundred and sixty men alive at once — four hundred of the common people, the sixty the leading lords of a province, simply prisoners of war. We have these accounts from the Spaniards themselves, for they not only admit it but boast of it and publish it. Could it have been as evidence of their justice or of their zeal for religion? Plainly these are means too different and too contrary to so holy an end. Had they really meant to spread our faith, they would have remembered that it does not grow by the gaining of territory but by the gaining of men; and they would have been more than satisfied with the killings necessary to war, without throwing in indiscriminately a slaughter, as on wild beasts, as universal as fire and sword could make it, sparing only — and on purpose — those they meant to make miserable slaves of for the work and service of their mines. So that many of the captains were put to death on the spot where they had made their conquest, by order of the kings of Castile, justly offended by the horror of their conduct, and almost all of them were hated and despised. God in his justice allowed that the whole of this huge plunder should be swallowed up by the sea in transit, or in the civil wars in which they devoured one another; and most of the men themselves were buried in a foreign land without any benefit from their victory.

That the revenue from these countries, even in the hands of so thrifty and so prudent a prince, falls so far short of what was promised to his predecessors, and of that original abundance of riches that was found at the first landing in those newly discovered lands (for though a great deal is brought back, we see it is nothing in comparison with what might have been expected), comes from the fact that the use of coin was entirely unknown there, and that as a result their gold was found heaped up all in one place, having no other use than for ornament and display, as a kind of furniture handed down from father to son by many mighty kings who were always working their mines to add to this vast pile of vessels and statues for the decoration of their palaces and temples. Whereas our gold is always in motion and in trade; we cut it up into a thousand small pieces, and cast it into a thousand forms, and scatter and disperse it in a thousand ways. But suppose our kings were to hoard up like that all the gold they could get over several generations, and let it lie idle.

Those of the kingdom of Mexico were in some ways more civilised and more advanced in the arts than the other nations around them. So they judged, as we do, that the world was nearing its end, and looked on the desolation we brought among them as a sure sign of it. They believed that the existence of the world was divided into five ages, and into the lives of five successive suns, of which four had already run their course, and that the one which was now giving them light was the fifth. The first perished, with all other living things, by a universal flood of water; the second by the heavens falling on us and suffocating every living thing — to this age they assigned the giants, and showed bones to the Spaniards from which, in proportion, men stood twenty feet tall; the third by fire, which burned and consumed everything; the fourth by a stirring of air and wind so violent that it brought down many mountains, in which men did not die, but were turned into baboons — what won't the weakness of human belief swallow? After the death of this fourth sun, the world was in perpetual darkness for twenty-five years; in the fifteenth of which a man and a woman were created, who restored the human race. Ten years later, on a certain day, the sun appeared newly created, and the count of their year takes its beginning from that day. The third day after its creation the ancient gods died, and the new ones have since been born one by one. How they think this last sun will perish, my author doesn't know; but their count of this fourth change tallies with the great conjunction of stars which, eight hundred and odd years ago, as astrologers suppose, produced great alterations and novelties in the world.

As for pomp and magnificence, on whose account I started this digression, neither Greece, Rome, nor Egypt can match, for utility, difficulty, or grandeur, any of their works against the highway to be seen in Peru, built by the kings of the country from the city of Quito to that of Cusco (three hundred leagues): straight, level, twenty-five paces wide, paved, and lined on both sides with high and beautiful walls; and close beside them, all along the inner side, two never-failing streams, edged with beautiful plants, which they call moly. In this work, where they ran into rocks and mountains, they cut them through and levelled them, and they filled up pits and valleys with stone and lime to bring them up to the level. At the end of every day's journey are beautiful palaces, stocked with provisions, clothing, and arms, both for travellers and for the armies that had to pass that way. In assessing this work I have taken into account the difficulty, which is especially considerable in that place: they used no stones less than ten feet square, and had no other means of transport than dragging their loads themselves by sheer arm-power, and they did not even know the art of scaffolding, or any other way of standing to work, except by throwing up earth against the building as it rose higher, and taking it away again when they had finished.

Let us come back to our coaches. Instead of these, and of every other kind of carriage, they had themselves carried on men's shoulders. This last king of Peru, on the day he was taken, was carried in this way between two bearers on staves of gold, and set in a chair of gold in the middle of his army. As many of these chair-men as were killed to bring him down (for the Spaniards meant to take him alive), so many others (and they contended for the privilege) took the place of those who had been killed, so that they could never bring him down, no matter what slaughter they made of these people, until a horseman seized him and brought him to the ground.
